title: Industrial and Automotive Supply Chain: What Connects Two Splitting Businesses
summary: Industrial and automotive supply chains are splitting at the corporate level. The operational work suppliers face on both sides has not changed.

# Industrial and Automotive Supply Chain: What Connects Two Splitting Businesses


By[Peter Spaulding](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/peter-spaulding) , *Sr. Content Writer*


Last Updated August 24, 2026


8 min read


In this article, learn about:


-


- Why Genuine Parts Company is separating its automotive and industrial businesses, and what it does not change


The four operational threads that run through both sides of the category


What changed at MSC Industrial Supply Co. after more than 3,000 suppliers moved to one data standard


Where to go next in[The Supply Chain Source](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/) for a closer look at any single thread


The industrial and automotive supply chain often looks like two businesses run by one team. A bearing sold to a maintenance buyer and a brake rotor sold through an auto parts chain reach different buyers. The corporate world is starting to treat them as separate too.


When it comes to operations, however, the same coordinator builds both shipments, the same catalog holds both part numbers, and the same customer requirements govern both invoices. This article maps what the two sides share and points to the deeper pieces on each thread.


## Why Is Genuine Parts Company Splitting Automotive and Industrial?


On Feb. 17, 2026, Genuine Parts Company[announced a plan to separate into two independent public companies](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/genuine-parts-company-announces-plan-to-separate-automotive-and-industrial-businesses-into-two-industry-leading-public-companies-302689075.html) . The automotive side, which includes NAPA Auto Parts, becomes Global Automotive. The industrial side becomes Global Industrial. The company said the split gives each business more focus and more control over how it spends capital.


The deal is structured to be tax free, and it does not need a shareholder vote. Completion is targeted for the first quarter of 2027. In a July 24, 2026 update, the company[said the split is still on track](https://www.digitalcommerce360.com/2026/07/24/genuine-parts-industrial-automotive-split-q2-earnings/) , with standalone audits done and investor days set for December.


One company with real scale on each side decided that two companies run better separately, though it may mean that suppliers now have to deal separately with each company.


## Does a Corporate Split Change How Suppliers Operate?


A corporate separation changes reporting lines, capital, and board structure. It does not change what a buyer asks a supplier to send, or how the supplier sends it. Ownership structure and operating structure are different things.


Most suppliers in this category run both product lines through one set of systems and one group of people. Order intake and the item catalog are shared. The warehouse that picks a hydraulic fitting on Tuesday picks a wheel hub on Wednesday, with the same labels and the same carrier appointments. If a customer splits in two, the number of relationships to manage can double, which raises the value of a shared operational core.


## What Threads Connect Industrial and Automotive Supply Chain Management?


Four operational threads run through both sides of this category. Each is a common source of chargebacks and late orders.


### OEM Versus Aftermarket Status


[Original equipment and aftermarket](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/supplier-connect-caterpillar-requirements-for-oem-and-aftermarket-channels) sales come with different terms. Original equipment manufacturer (OEM) programs bring qualification steps, documented process controls, and tight delivery windows. Aftermarket programs weigh catalog breadth, fitment accuracy, and stock levels more heavily. Many suppliers serve both, so one team works from two rulebooks.


### Parts Identification and Fitment Data


Automotive suppliers work with two standards from the Auto Care Association.[ACES, the Aftermarket Catalog Exchange Standard, holds fitment data](https://www.autocare.org/data-standards) , the record of which vehicles a part fits.[PIES, the Product Information Exchange Standard](https://www.autocare.org/pies) , holds product details such as descriptions, attributes, packaging, and images. Shared databases sit behind both, and the current releases are ACES 5.0 and PIES 8.0.


Industrial suppliers rarely use ACES and PIES, but they hit the same wall from another direction. Manufacturer, customer, and distributor part numbers all describe one item, and they rarely agree. When those records drift apart, orders go against the wrong number and returns arrive without a match.


### Long-Tail Inventory and Industrial Distribution Trends


Both sides carry deep catalogs, and a large share of[stock-keeping units (SKUs)](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/what-is-a-stock-keeping-unit-sku) sell in single digits per year. A discontinued vehicle still needs parts, and a 20-year-old machine still needs a seal kit. That long tail creates a familiar set of problems:


-


- Forecasting on very thin sales history


Choosing what to stock in a distribution center (DC) and what to dropship


Explaining fill-rate misses on items nobody expected to move


Industrial distribution trends can show which parts of the tail are growing. They do not make a slow-moving SKU easier to forecast.


**Related Reading:**[What Is SKU Rationalization?](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/sku-rationalization)


### Oversized, Hazmat, and Warranty Compliance


Industrial and automotive goods carry more paperwork than most consumer categories:


-


- [Freight class](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/re-classifications-and-re-weighs-for-freight-shipping) and handling rules apply to heavy and oversized items


Lubricants, batteries, aerosols, and adhesives fall under hazardous materials rules, each with its own labeling


Core returns and warranty programs add records that tie back to the original sale
